Maladaptive Strategies.value: Making any plans for the future

Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

issues.item: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: 'Perpetrator' cues are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma being an unexpected/traumatic death of a loved one; this wording implies an assaultive interpersonal trauma rather than bereavement-related PTSD.

issues.item: Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
issues.explanation: 'Safe seat seeking' fits fear of immediate interpersonal attack or entrapment more than traumatic bereavement. In combination with startle/hypervigilance, it shifts the profile toward assault-type threat rather than loss-related PTSD, with no supporting trauma-specific content elsewhere.

vignette:
Arjun was a 20-year-old South Asian writer who had come for help after months in which the death of his older sister had come to shape nearly every part of his life. She had died unexpectedly in a road accident on her way home from work, and because the call came late at night, the memory that stayed with him was not a clear picture but the abrupt sound of his phone vibrating on the desk beside his unfinished draft, followed by his mother’s voice breaking before she had fully said what had happened. In the weeks after the funeral, Arjun found himself staring at the blank pages of his notebook and feeling as if the future had been stolen along with her. He had once imagined finishing school, publishing his writing, and eventually moving out; now he said he could not make even small plans without a wave of dread. When friends asked about holidays, classes, or deadlines, he would deflect, not because he was indifferent, but because planning felt to him like tempting fate. He kept asking his mother, a cousin, and sometimes even a close classmate to tell him he was okay, asking the same questions again if the first answer did not settle him. Anything that reminded him of his sister—a song she liked, the smell of the tea she used to make, a scarf left hanging near the door—was pushed away, hidden, or avoided entirely.

As Arjun made sense of what had happened, his thoughts hardened into a set of painful conclusions. He had come to believe that he used to be a happy person, and that the accident had ended that part of him; now, in his words, he was “always miserable.” More deeply, he felt that the world had become a dangerous place and that his beliefs about how life worked had been completely destroyed. People could be fine one moment and gone the next; plans, safety, and ordinary routines no longer seemed trustworthy. Because of those beliefs, he began to treat future plans as dangerous in themselves, as if writing them down would invite another loss. He avoided setting goals for his work as a writer, stopped agreeing to social events weeks in advance, and even hesitated when offered a stable freelance opportunity because committing to it felt unbearably final. Each time he withdrew or sought reassurance, the relief lasted only briefly, and then the same conclusions returned with more force: if he could not tolerate imagining tomorrow, it must be because tomorrow was not safe. The more he tried to get others to reassure him or to steer around anything connected to grief, the more convinced he became that he had lost his former self for good.

Those same beliefs also kept his body in a constant state of alarm. Arjun said he could not relax even when he knew he was in a safe place, and his apartment, his classroom, even the quiet café where he sometimes wrote all felt unsettled to him. He jumped at ordinary sounds—a delivery truck slamming a tailgate, a door closing too sharply, a phone buzzing on the table—and his sleep became fragmented, with trouble falling asleep and waking several times through the night. He would lie there replaying the call about his sister, or picturing his mother’s voice, and his mind seemed unable to let go of the idea that something terrible could happen again. After a night of little sleep, his fear of the world felt even more believable, and the sense that life was unsafe made him more likely to avoid planning, more likely to seek reassurance, and more likely to scan for reminders of loss. In that way, his efforts to protect himself only fed the very misery and sense of danger he hated. As the months passed, his writing suffered; he missed deadlines, stopped replying promptly to editors, and declined invitations to read at a campus event because he could not imagine standing in front of people and pretending he was all right.

By the time he sought therapy, Arjun was exhausted by the narrowness of the life he had built around not being hurt again. He had come after a night when a car backfiring outside his building jolted him awake and left him lying in bed, shaking, unable to settle, and then the next morning he caught himself asking his cousin for the third time whether he seemed “normal.” What he feared most was that this version of him—miserable, guarded, unable to trust the future—had become permanent, and what he most hoped for was some way to remember his sister without feeling that every reminder or plan would open the same unbearable wound.
